title: When a marriage was never — or need not remain — valid
subtitle: Void and voidable marriages under ss 11–13 Matrimonial Causes Act 1973
objectives: State the void/voidable distinction and explain its practical consequences — who may apply, whether there is a time limit, and what a decree of nullity actually does in each case
List the s 11 grounds on which a marriage is void and the s 12 grounds on which a marriage is voidable, and explain the s 13 bars to relief
Apply the void/voidable distinction and the s 13 bars to a new fact pattern, and identify which ground (if any) is available on the facts

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the grounds on which a marriage is void — treated as never having existed
Sets out the grounds on which a marriage is voidable — valid unless and until annulled by the court
Sets out the bars to relief that can prevent a decree of nullity being granted even where a s 12 ground is made out

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Nullity gets less exam attention than divorce, which makes it a reliable place for a question to hide a trap: students who can recite the grounds often mix up which ones make a marriage void and which merely voidable, and miss the bars to relief entirely. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You can list the grounds — this lesson checks whether you can sort them correctly and spot when a bar defeats an otherwise good claim.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. Expect scenario questions that require you to classify a ground as void or voidable and then check it against the s 13 bars.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about the void/voidable split before moving on — every later part in this lesson assumes you can place a ground correctly into one category or the other.

overview.hook: Not every marriage that looks valid on the day is valid in law, and not every marriage that is valid in law has to stay that way. Nullity is the law's answer to both problems — but it answers them differently depending on which kind of defect is involved. Some defects mean a marriage never legally existed at all, whatever the ceremony looked like. Others leave a fully valid marriage standing, unless and until one of the parties chooses to have it annulled. Confusing the two is the most common way to lose easy marks in this area.

parts.heading: Two very different kinds of defective marriage
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: English law recognises two categories of defective marriage, and the whole of this lesson is organised around keeping them apart. A void marriage is treated, in law, as never having existed at all — the defect is fundamental enough that no valid marriage was ever formed, whatever the ceremony looked like on the day. A voidable marriage, by contrast, is a fully valid marriage unless and until a court annuls it — the defect gives one party the right to apply to end it, but until that application succeeds the marriage exists and has full legal effect.

That distinction drives several practical consequences that examiners test directly. A void marriage requires no decree to have legal effect — its nullity is automatic, in the sense that the law never treated it as a marriage — though the parties (or, importantly, any other person with a sufficient interest, such as a third party affected by a question of inheritance) will usually still seek a decree of nullity for the certainty and financial remedies that come with a formal court order. There is no time limit for seeking that decree, and it can be sought even after one party has died, because there is no valid marriage to be preserved by delay.

A voidable marriage is different in every one of those respects. Only the parties to the marriage can apply for it to be annulled — no third party has standing. The application must generally be brought within strict time limits set by s 13(2). And because the marriage was valid until annulled, questions like the status of children born during it, or property acquired during it, are approached on the basis that a real marriage existed for as long as it lasted.

One practical point links both categories: financial remedies on divorce under Part II of the 1973 Act are also available on a decree of nullity, whether the marriage was void or voidable. Nullity is not simply 'divorce's smaller cousin with no financial consequences' — the same statutory machinery for sorting out money and property applies.

components.definition: A marriage treated in law as never having existed, because of a fundamental defect (e.g. bigamy, a prohibited relationship, or a formality failure). No decree is legally required to establish its invalidity, there is no time limit for seeking one, and any person with a sufficient interest may apply.

A marriage that is fully valid unless and until annulled by court decree, because of a defect going to the quality of the parties' consent or capacity at the time (e.g. non-consummation, duress, or a pre-existing condition). Only the parties may apply, and the application is subject to the time limits and bars in s 13.

interaction.prompt: Can a person who was never a party to the marriage apply for a decree of nullity on the ground that the marriage was void?
options: Yes — any person with a sufficient interest may apply, since a void marriage never legally existed
No — only the two parties to the marriage may ever apply for a decree of nullity
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Standing is one of the clearest practical differences between the two categories — void marriages can be challenged by an interested third party; voidable marriages cannot.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. For a void marriage, standing is wider than for a voidable one — any person with a sufficient interest, not just the parties, can seek a decree, because a void marriage never had legal existence to begin with.

parts.heading: The grounds that make a marriage void
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, working through the statute
body: Section 11 of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 sets out the void grounds, and all of them share a common feature: each one reflects a defect so fundamental that the law refuses to recognise any marriage as having come into being at all.

The first ground catches marriages that were never valid under the Marriage Acts in the first place — most importantly, marriages between parties within the prohibited degrees of relationship (close family members), and marriages solemnized in serious disregard of the required formalities. The second ground is bigamy: a marriage is void if either party was already lawfully married, or already a civil partner of someone else, at the time of the ceremony — the earlier relationship simply has priority, and the later 'marriage' never existed in law. A third, now largely historical, ground applied where the parties were not respectively male and female — spent, in practice, since the 2013 Act made same-sex marriage lawful, though it remains on the statute book for marriages that predate that change. A fourth, narrower ground applies to certain polygamous marriages entered into abroad where a party was domiciled in England and Wales at the time.

Notice what unites these: capacity defects (bigamy, prohibited relationship) and serious formality defects both belong here, in the void category — not the voidable one. That is the single most tested distinction in this part of the syllabus, because it is tempting to assume any 'problem with the wedding itself' is automatically void and any 'problem discovered afterwards' is automatically voidable. The next part shows why that shortcut breaks down.

components.text: A marriage celebrated after 31st July 1971... shall be void on the following grounds only, that is to say— (a) that it is not a valid marriage under the provisions of the Marriage Acts 1949 to 1986 (that is to say where— (i) the parties are within the prohibited degrees of relationship; (ii) either party is under the age required by law for marriage; or (iii) the parties have intermarried in disregard of certain requirements as to the formation of marriage); (b) that at the time of the marriage either party was already lawfully married or a civil partner of another person; (c) [in the case of a polygamous marriage entered into outside England and Wales] that either party was at the time of the marriage domiciled in England and Wales.
elements: Below the legal minimum age for marriage
Serious disregard of the required formalities
Bigamy — either party already married or in a civil partnership
Certain polygamous marriages entered into abroad where a party is domiciled in England and Wales

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that makes this marriage void rather than voidable.
interaction.scenarioText: Daniel married Freya in a register office ceremony last spring. Unknown to Freya, Daniel had never divorced his first wife, whom he married eight years earlier in Scotland and never legally separated from.
tappableSpans: married Freya in a register office ceremony
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. This is bigamy under s 11(b) — Daniel was already lawfully married when he 'married' Freya, so the second marriage is void, not merely voidable, regardless of Freya's lack of knowledge.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that goes to capacity to marry at all, not to consent or knowledge. Daniel being already married is bigamy under s 11(b), which makes the second marriage void outright.

parts.heading: The voidable grounds: consummation, consent and capacity at the time
parts.voice: clinical — treats sensitive grounds soberly and without sensationalism
body: Section 12 lists the voidable grounds, and the tone this part takes matters: these grounds concern intimate and sometimes distressing matters, and the law's approach is deliberately clinical rather than moralistic. A marriage is voidable, not automatically ended, because the underlying relationship was genuinely formed — the defect concerns the quality of consent or capacity at the time, not whether a marriage came into being at all.

Two grounds concern consummation, and it matters which applies. Non-consummation due to either party's incapacity is available regardless of fault. Non-consummation due to the respondent's wilful refusal requires the petitioner to show the respondent has, without reasonable excuse, refused to consummate the marriage. Both grounds are, by statute, available only in respect of opposite-sex marriages — the 2013 Act deliberately did not extend either ground to same-sex marriages, on the view that a legal test built around specific opposite-sex sexual conduct did not translate coherently to same-sex relationships.

A further ground covers lack of valid consent — where either party did not validly consent to the marriage, whether through duress, mistake, unsoundness of mind, or otherwise. Duress here has been interpreted broadly by the courts in recent decades to include not only physical threats but a genuine overbearing of the will through psychological pressure — the key question is whether the party's will was truly overborne, not merely whether they were reluctant.

The remaining grounds are narrower and largely historical in how often they are litigated: that either party, though capable of validly consenting, was suffering from a mental disorder making them unfitted for marriage; that the respondent was suffering from a venereal disease in a communicable form at the time of the marriage; that the respondent was pregnant by someone other than the petitioner at the time of the marriage; and two grounds added following the Gender Recognition Act 2004, concerning an interim gender recognition certificate or a subsequently acquired gender.

components.text: A marriage celebrated after 31st July 1971... shall be voidable on the following grounds only, that is to say— (a) that the marriage has not been consummated owing to the incapacity of either party to consummate it; (b) that the marriage has not been consummated owing to the wilful refusal of the respondent to consummate it; (c) that either party to the marriage did not validly consent to it, whether in consequence of duress, mistake, unsoundness of mind or otherwise; (d) that at the time of the marriage either party, though capable of giving a valid consent, was suffering (whether continuously or intermittently) from mental disorder ... of such a kind or to such an extent as to be unfitted for marriage.
elements: Non-consummation due to incapacity — no fault required, opposite-sex marriages only
Non-consummation due to wilful refusal of the respondent — opposite-sex marriages only
Lack of valid consent — duress, mistake, unsoundness of mind or otherwise
Mental disorder rendering a party unfitted for marriage despite capacity to consent

interaction.prompt: In the passage below explaining the modern approach to duress, highlight the sentence that states the correct test.
interaction.passage: Older authorities asked only whether the petitioner reasonably feared for life, limb or liberty before finding duress. The modern approach is broader: the court asks whether the petitioner's will was truly overborne by pressure, of whatever kind, so that the consent given was not genuine — psychological pressure from a family member can suffice, even without any threat of physical harm.
interaction.ratioSentence: The modern approach is broader: the court asks whether the petitioner's will was truly overborne by pressure, of whatever kind, so that the consent given was not genuine — psychological pressure from a family member can suffice, even without any threat of physical harm.

parts.heading: The bars to relief under s 13
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: Making out a s 12 ground is not the end of the analysis — it only gets you to the point where the court can consider a decree. Section 13 sets out bars that apply only to voidable marriages, and missing them is the second most common way students lose marks in this topic, right after mixing up void and voidable grounds in the first place.

The general bar in s 13(1) is sometimes called the approbation bar: the court must not grant a decree if the respondent satisfies the court that the petitioner, knowing it was open to have the marriage avoided, behaved in a way that led the respondent reasonably to believe the petitioner would not seek to do so — and that it would be unjust to the respondent to grant the decree now. In plain terms: if you knew about the defect, carried on as if the marriage were unaffected for long enough that your spouse reasonably relied on that, the law can shut the door on you later changing your mind.

Section 13(2) adds a strict time limit for several of the grounds — lack of consent, mental disorder, venereal disease, and pregnancy by another — requiring proceedings to be instituted within three years of the marriage (subject to limited leave to bring a late application in mental-disorder cases). Section 13(3) adds a further, narrower bar specific to the venereal disease and pregnancy grounds: the petitioner must not have known the relevant fact at the time of the marriage. Crucially, none of the s 13 bars apply to a void marriage at all — there is no time limit and no approbation bar for bigamy, a prohibited relationship, or a formality failure, precisely because a void marriage never existed for delay to legitimise.

components.text: (1) The court shall not... grant a decree of nullity on the ground that a marriage is voidable if the respondent satisfies the court— (a) that the petitioner, with knowledge that it was open to him to have the marriage avoided, so conducted himself in relation to the respondent as to lead the respondent reasonably to believe that he would not seek to do so; and (b) that it would be unjust to the respondent to grant the decree. (2) ... the court shall not grant a decree of nullity by virtue of section 12(c), (d), (e), (f) or (g) ... unless it is satisfied that proceedings were instituted within the period of three years from the date of the marriage.
elements: Approbation bar — knowledge plus conduct plus reasonable reliance plus injustice, s 13(1)
Three-year time limit for consent, mental disorder, disease and pregnancy grounds, s 13(2)
Additional bar for venereal disease and pregnancy: petitioner must not have known the fact at the time, s 13(3)
None of the s 13 bars apply to a void marriage under s 11

interaction.prompt: A petitioner seeks a decree of nullity on the ground of non-consummation due to wilful refusal, four years after the marriage. Is the time limit in s 13(2) an obstacle to this application?
options: No — s 13(2)'s three-year time limit applies to certain other s 12 grounds, but not to either consummation ground under s 12(a) or (b)
Yes — every s 12 ground is subject to the three-year time limit without exception
No — because non-consummation is a void ground, not a voidable one
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Section 13(2) lists specific paragraphs of s 12 — consent, mental disorder, disease, pregnancy — and the consummation grounds under s 12(a) and (b) are not among them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check which paragraphs s 13(2) actually lists. It applies to lack of consent, mental disorder, venereal disease and pregnancy by another — not to either consummation ground, which remains a voidable (not void) ground under s 12(a)/(b).

parts.heading: Choosing nullity over divorce
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by justifying its own place in practice
body: It is worth asking, briefly, why anyone chooses nullity over divorce when the marriage was voidable rather than void — since divorce is now available on a simple, no-fault basis (Lesson 3). The answer is usually personal rather than strategic: some petitioners want a decree that reflects a belief the marriage was never a real one in substance — for instance, where it was never consummated, or where consent was genuinely absent — rather than a decree that simply records the marriage's breakdown after a period of being validly married. Religious considerations matter for some petitioners too: certain religious authorities treat annulment and divorce very differently for the purposes of remarriage within that faith.

For a void marriage, by contrast, there often isn't a live choice at all — divorce presupposes a valid marriage to end, so a party who believes their marriage was void (bigamy, a prohibited relationship, an under-age ceremony) has no divorce route available and must seek a decree of nullity, or simply proceed as if no marriage existed, if the point is not disputed.

The exam skill this lesson is really building is classification under pressure: read the facts, decide void or voidable, check the specific paragraph, then check whether a s 13 bar defeats it. Skipping any one of those four steps is where marks are lost — not from not knowing the law, but from not applying it in the right order.

components.label: The four-step nullity checklist
points: 1. Is there a defect at all, and when did it arise — at formation, or discovered afterwards?
2. Does the defect fall within s 11 (void) or s 12 (voidable)?
3. If voidable, which specific s 12 paragraph applies, and are its own conditions met (e.g. wilful refusal without reasonable excuse)?
4. If voidable, check the s 13 bars — approbation, the three-year limit, and (for disease/pregnancy) the petitioner's lack of prior knowledge

interaction.prompt: Leila married Karim five years ago. She has just discovered that, throughout their marriage, Karim knew he could seek an annulment because the marriage had never been consummated owing to Leila's incapacity, but he told her repeatedly he was happy for things to stay as they were and never mentioned annulment until now, when he wants to remarry. Karim applies for a decree of nullity. Analyse whether the application is likely to succeed.
factsToOrder: The marriage has not been consummated owing to Leila's incapacity
Karim knew for years that annulment was available to him
Karim repeatedly told Leila he was happy for things to stay as they were
Karim now applies for a decree, five years after the marriage, because he wants to remarry

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Karim's application for a decree of nullity on the ground of non-consummation due to incapacity is barred under s 13.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 12(a) makes non-consummation due to either party's incapacity a voidable ground. Section 13(1) bars a decree where the respondent shows the petitioner knew avoidance was open, conducted himself so as to lead the respondent reasonably to believe he would not seek it, and that it would now be unjust to grant the decree. Non-consummation grounds are not subject to the three-year time limit in s 13(2).
modelAnswer.application: Karim has a s 12(a) ground available in principle, and it is not time-barred, since s 13(2) does not apply to consummation grounds. But Karim knew about the ground for years and repeatedly reassured Leila he was content with things as they stood — precisely the conduct s 13(1) targets. Leila has reasonably relied on that reassurance in continuing the marriage, and it would plausibly be unjust to allow Karim to reverse course now, years later, for reasons unconnected to the original ground.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Karim's application is likely to be barred under s 13(1), notwithstanding that the underlying s 12(a) ground is made out and not time-barred.

testPool.prompt: Name the statutory section that lists the grounds on which a marriage is void.
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 11 of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973.

testPool.prompt: Name the two consummation grounds under s 12 MCA 1973, and state which category of marriage they cannot be used for.
acceptableAnswers: incapacity and wilful refusal; not available for same-sex marriages
non-consummation by incapacity and by wilful refusal; unavailable for same-sex marriage
testPool.modelAnswer: Non-consummation due to incapacity (s 12(a)) and non-consummation due to wilful refusal (s 12(b)); neither ground is available to annul a same-sex marriage.

testPool.prompt: Is a decree of nullity legally required before a void marriage is treated as having no legal effect?
options: No — a void marriage is void automatically, though a decree is usually still sought for certainty and financial remedies
Yes — without a decree, a void marriage remains fully valid indefinitely

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is a voidable, not void, ground under the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973?
options: The parties are within the prohibited degrees of relationship
Either party was already lawfully married at the time of the ceremony
Either party did not validly consent to the marriage owing to duress
Either party was under the minimum legal age for marriage
testPool.trapExplanation: The other three options are all s 11 void grounds — prohibited degrees, bigamy and under-age marriage all go to the fundamental capacity or formality of the marriage. Lack of valid consent through duress is a s 12(c) voidable ground: the marriage was genuinely formed, but the quality of consent was defective.

testPool.prompt: Two years after their wedding, Nadia discovers her husband Robert was already a civil partner of someone else when they married, and that relationship was never legally dissolved. Which is the correct classification and time limit?
options: Void under s 11(b); no time limit applies to seeking a decree
Voidable under s 12(c); a three-year time limit applies from the date of the marriage
Void under s 11(b), but Nadia must apply within three years like any other nullity ground
testPool.trapExplanation: Bigamy — including where the earlier relationship is a civil partnership rather than a marriage — is a void ground under s 11(b), and none of the s 13 bars (including the three-year time limit) apply to void grounds at all.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court follows when analysing a nullity claim.
items: Identify the alleged defect in the marriage
Classify the defect as falling within s 11 (void) or s 12 (voidable)
If voidable, check the specific s 12 ground's own conditions are met
If voidable, check whether any s 13 bar defeats the claim

testPool.prompt: Order these statements about the s 13(1) approbation bar correctly, from the first thing the respondent must show to the last.
items: The petitioner knew it was open to him or her to have the marriage avoided
The petitioner's conduct led the respondent reasonably to believe he would not seek to avoid it
It would now be unjust to the respondent to grant the decree

testPool.prompt: Under s 13(3), what additional condition applies specifically to the venereal disease and pregnancy-by-another grounds, beyond the general three-year time limit?
options: The petitioner must not have known the relevant fact at the time of the marriage
The respondent must admit the fact in open court
The couple must never have lived together after the marriage
testPool.explanation: Section 13(3) adds that a decree cannot be granted on these two grounds unless the petitioner was unaware of the relevant fact (the disease, or the pregnancy by another) at the time of the marriage — knowingly marrying with that knowledge forecloses the ground.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact most relevant to whether the s 13(1) approbation bar applies here.
testPool.scenarioText: Six months after their wedding, Grace learns the marriage was never consummated owing to her husband's incapacity. She says nothing for two years, continuing to introduce him as her husband and never raising the issue, before suddenly applying for a decree of nullity when she meets someone else.
tappableSpans: never consummated owing to her husband's incapacity
continuing to introduce him as her husband
applying for a decree of nullity when she meets someone else
testPool.correctSpan: continuing to introduce him as her husband
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Grace's conduct over the two years of apparent normalcy — despite knowing the ground was available — is exactly the kind of conduct s 13(1) targets: it may have led her husband reasonably to believe she would not seek annulment.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The approbation bar turns on the petitioner's conduct after learning of the ground, not on the ground itself or on why she eventually applied. Look for the fact showing continued, apparently normal married life despite her knowledge.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario describes a void marriage rather than a voidable one?
testPool.scenarioA: A woman marries her uncle, not realising English law treats this as within the prohibited degrees of relationship.
testPool.scenarioB: A man discovers, on his wedding night, that his new wife is unable to consummate the marriage owing to a longstanding medical condition.
testPool.explanation: A is a prohibited-degrees case under s 11(a) — void, regardless of the parties' knowledge or intentions. B is a s 12(a) consummation ground — voidable, and subject to the s 13 bars, including the three-year time limit.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is time-barred under s 13(2), assuming no other bar applies?
testPool.scenarioA: A petitioner applies for a decree on the ground of lack of valid consent through duress, four years after the marriage.
testPool.scenarioB: A petitioner applies for a decree on the ground of non-consummation due to the respondent's wilful refusal, four years after the marriage.
testPool.explanation: Lack of consent under s 12(c) is one of the grounds listed in s 13(2), so the three-year time limit applies and four years is too late. Wilful refusal under s 12(b) is a consummation ground, which s 13(2) does not cover, so B is not time-barred on that basis alone.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that any person with a sufficient interest — not just the parties — can seek a decree of nullity on a voidable ground?
sliderLabels: Definitely — standing is open to any interested party
Definitely not — only the parties to the marriage can apply
testPool.correctPosition: only the parties to the marriage can apply
testPool.explanation: Only the parties to the marriage can apply to annul a voidable marriage. Wide standing for third parties is a feature of void marriages only, because a void marriage never had legal existence to protect.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the s 13 bars to relief can ever apply to a void marriage under s 11?
sliderLabels: Confident — the bars can defeat a void claim too
Confident — the bars never apply to void marriages
testPool.correctPosition: the bars never apply to void marriages
testPool.explanation: The s 13 bars — approbation and the time limits — apply only to voidable marriages under s 12. There is no equivalent bar for void grounds under s 11; delay or apparent acceptance cannot validate a marriage that never legally existed.

testPool.prompt: A petitioner seeks a decree of nullity on the ground that the respondent was suffering from a venereal disease, in a communicable form, at the time of the marriage — and the petitioner knew this at the time but married anyway. Is the s 13(3) bar likely to defeat the claim?
options: Yes — s 13(3) requires the petitioner not to have known the relevant fact at the time of the marriage, and here the petitioner knew
No — s 13(3) only applies to the pregnancy ground, not the disease ground
No — knowledge is irrelevant to any nullity ground
testPool.explanation: Section 13(3) applies to both the venereal disease ground and the pregnancy-by-another ground, and requires the petitioner's ignorance of the relevant fact at the time of the marriage — knowingly marrying despite the fact forecloses reliance on it later.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating every 'defect discovered after the wedding' as automatically voidable, and every 'defect with the ceremony itself' as automatically void. The correct classification depends on which specific paragraph of s 11 or s 12 the facts fit — and even a correctly classified voidable ground can still fail if a s 13 bar applies.
